newsitem.title: USA: NYSE against linking NASD with traditional trading.
newsitem.headline: NYSE against linking NASD with traditional trading.

text.p: The New York Stock Exchange opposes linking National Association of Securities Dealers' trading with traditional stock exchanges through the Intermarket Trading System (ITS), according to a letter released here on Tuesday.

"These market differences continue to exist and we continue to question whether it is possible to integrate these fundamentally different markets," the big board wrote in a June 26 letter to the Securities and Exchange Commission.
The letter was released by the SEC.

The exchange's comments come a month after the SEC asked the nation's stock exchanges to improve ITS, a system established in 1978 which allows trades in NYSE-listed stocks and others to be conducted elsewhere.

The agency asked the NYSE, American Stock Exchange and others to do away with what it called "anti-competitive" practices and questioned whether or not over-the-counter dealer trades via the NASD's automated quoting system can be integrated with exchange auction markets.
Among other things, the SEC in May faulted the system for imposing standard trading increments, which it said inhibits exchanges from using narrower trading increments including decimals.

But members of the ITS in a separate June 26 letter asserted that the agency's concerns about trading increments are moot and that participants have been "responsive to the competitive initiatives of individual participants."
"We believe that the participants have always addressed issues regarding minimum increments in a timely and pragmatic manner," the ITS exchanges wrote.

In its letter, the NYSE warned that allowing NASD to participate in the linking system would be difficult if not impossible. The exchange said in the past the exchanges "have questioned the appropriateness of linking with a market that has fundamentally different trade reporting rules."
Further, the NYSE said ITS participants have doubted the NASD's monitoring and surveillance capabilities.
"We understnad that the Commission historically has not shared our level of concern," the NYSE wrote.
